newsitem.title: USA: U.S. pork exports seen up 30 pct in 1997.
newsitem.headline: U.S. pork exports seen up 30 pct in 1997.

text.p: The U.S. Agriculture Department Wednesday forecast U.S. pork exports would be up 30 percent in 1997 from the prior year, fuelled by expected increases in shipments to Japan, Korea, Hong Kong, Mexico and Russia.

The U.S. exported 793 million pounds of pork during Jan-Oct 1996, up 22 percent from the prior year, with almost 90 percent of the gain due to increased shipments to Japan, a report by USDA's Economic Research Service said.
"Japan remains the pre-eminent customer of U.S. exporters, accounting in 1996 for over 55 percent of total U.S. pork shipments," the report said.

It said the expiration of a special import tariff on pork known as the Safeguard (SG) mechanism on April 1, a World Trade Organization mandated reduction of the import tariff rate to 4.7 percent, the traditional Japanese spring holidays and anticipation of SG removal on July 1 will "drive U.S. exports to Japan in spring 1997."
USDA said it expects a re-imposition of SG in the third quarter of Japanese fiscal year 1997-98.

The department forecast 1997 U.S. pork production would be about even with 1996 at around 17.1 billion pounds, based on the market hog inventory, pig crops and farrowing intentions reported in December.
It said projected pork production in the first quarter is 4.2 billion pounds, down four percent from a year earlier.
USDA said continued moderate economic growth, a sharp export increase and lower per capita supplies are expected to boost 1997 hog prices about $2 per cwt above 1996's $53.45.
